tasks.purpose: 就公共图书馆的开放时间表达立场
tasks.setting: In many towns, public libraries are used by people who work or study during the day. Some people believe that local councils should keep these libraries open on weekday evenings, even if doing so means reducing the hours available on weekday mornings.
tasks.lead: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
bullets: Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
must: 明确回应延长工作日晚间开放时间并缩短上午开放时间的主张，以解释和相关例证支持立场。
tasks.model:
Public libraries serve people with very different daily routines. The proposal to exchange some morning opening hours for evening access would help those who are occupied during the day, but it could also exclude other users. I agree that libraries should open on some weekday evenings, provided that councils retain a reliable morning service.

Evening access would make a valuable public resource available to people who cannot easily visit during working hours. A parent employed full time, for example, might otherwise have only a brief opportunity at the weekend to borrow books or use a computer with a child. An evening session would give that family another choice and could also benefit students who need a quiet place after school. Since library buildings already exist, changing the timetable may allow councils to reach these groups without building additional facilities.

Nevertheless, taking too many hours from the morning would simply transfer the inconvenience to another group. Retired residents, carers with young children and people whose work begins later may depend on a predictable morning visit. For a person who uses library computers to complete forms, a closure could mean postponing an important task. Councils should therefore examine local patterns of use and keep at least some mornings open. Staff could also seek feedback after a trial period rather than assuming that the same timetable suits every neighbourhood.

In conclusion, I support shifting part of the schedule towards weekday evenings because it can widen access for workers and students. The change should be limited and reviewed, however, so that people who rely on morning opening do not lose a service they already use.

tasks.purpose: 就中学的交通教育表达立场
tasks.setting: Some people argue that all secondary schools should require students to travel to school by public transport at least once a week. They believe that this requirement would teach young people to use local transport independently and encourage them to make fewer journeys by car.
tasks.lead: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
bullets: Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
must: 明确回应所有中学生每周至少一次乘公共交通上学的要求，以解释和相关例证支持立场。
tasks.model:
Learning to use public transport can give young people greater independence and may reduce reliance on cars. Nevertheless, I disagree with requiring every secondary school pupil to use it once a week. The proposal overlooks differences in local services and in pupils' circumstances, although schools can still teach the same skills in less rigid ways.

The most obvious difficulty is that public transport is not equally available to all families. A pupil in a town may have several bus routes within walking distance, whereas one in a rural area may have no suitable service at the time lessons begin. Even when a route exists, an indirect journey with several changes may add considerably to the school day. Requiring the same weekly journey from both pupils would therefore impose unequal burdens rather than offer equal opportunities.

There are also individual needs that a general rule cannot accommodate. Some pupils have disabilities or caring responsibilities that make a particular journey difficult. Families may also find regular fares expensive. Instead of enforcing a weekly trip, schools could include practical lessons on reading timetables, planning accessible routes and buying tickets. Where a suitable service exists, a supervised class visit could let pupils practise these skills without requiring every family to reorganise its routine.

Such teaching would not guarantee a permanent reduction in car use, since that depends partly on the quality and price of transport. It could, however, give pupils the knowledge to choose a bus or train when one is practical. In conclusion, transport education is worthwhile, but a universal weekly travel requirement is too inflexible. Schools should teach route planning and provide opportunities to practise while taking local and individual circumstances into account.
